title: Muse’s Phone Test: Human Cast Members Stand In for AI
part1:
Asking AI to call a store feels like a glimpse of a convenient future. But in Meta’s Muse test, AI was not always the one making the call. In some calls, trained contract staff called as human concierges and completed the conversation with the other person.

Muse is an AI agent that can handle requests by phone, such as booking a haircut or checking whether a product is in stock. But AI was not the only one taking the stage on the phone. In effect, human cast members appeared from behind an AI that had been handed a script.
part2:
What is needed here is an explanation of the roles. Does the person receiving the call clearly learn who is speaking? Meta executives admitted that starting a test in which contract staff made calls without proper disclosure was a “mistake.” A phone call is not a two-person scene involving only the person who made the request and the service. There is also the person receiving the call.

Moreover, making a call work may require user information. Meta employees worried that sensitive information might be shared with contract staff without users intending it. This is not a story about a large-scale information leak having taken place. Still, it can be hard to tell from the audience whether information given to AI is also passed to a human worker.
part3:
Meta temporarily rolled back the human concierge feature. It did not stop Muse as a whole. It plans to keep improving the phone feature and release it only when it is ready and proper disclosure can be made.

What was at issue with making calls on users’ behalf was not only whether the task could be completed. It was also who would speak and what information would be used. If the task is passed to a person, that too should be made clear to the other party. A convenient phone play seems to require planning that includes all of this.
in_one_line: Meta’s Muse test sometimes used human contractors instead of AI to make calls, without clearly informing recipients.
